svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Amazon Macie's automated sensitive data discovery selects objects for analysis and what a sensitivity score therefore asserts. A daily cycle evaluates the S3 inventory to identify eligible objects and selects a sampling of representative objects. The sampling technique groups objects that have similar metadata and are likely to have similar content, by dimensions such as bucket name, prefix, storage class, file name extension and last modified date, then selects a representative set of samples from each group, retrieves the latest version of each selected object, analyses it, and discards its copy when the analysis completes. The strategy prioritises distributed analyses using a breadth-first approach across the data estate, selecting objects each day from as many general purpose buckets as possible, so a bucket not yet analysed is a higher priority than one already found to contain sensitive data, and results can begin to appear within forty-eight hours depending on the size of the estate. An object previously analysed and unchanged since is not analysed again. AWS states that any single object sample is not guaranteed to be conclusive. A sensitivity score is defined as a quantitative measure of the intersection of two dimensions: the amount of sensitive data Macie has found in a bucket and the amount of data Macie has analysed in a bucket. The central ambiguity is that the value fifty carries two unrelated meanings: on first enabling automated discovery every bucket is assigned a score of fifty with the Not yet analysed label, and separately, where a bucket's permissions settings prevent Macie from accessing it or its objects, the score is also fifty with the same label, so a queue position and a permission failure appear as the same row and only coverage data distinguishes them. Empty buckets are the exception, receiving a score of one and the Not sensitive label. Finding no sensitive data in an object decreases the bucket score, finding sensitive data increases it, and detections are removed from the score if the object is later changed or deleted. A score and label do not imply the criticality or importance the bucket may have for the organisation, and a calculated score can be overridden by manually assigning the maximum of one hundred, which sets the label to Sensitive. Four populations sit outside the picture: objects that are not classifiable because of storage class or file name extension, objects encrypted with a key Macie cannot access and is not allowed to use, up to one thousand buckets excluded by choice, and entire Regions where automated discovery was never enabled, since settings apply only to the current Region. In an organisation the administrator's settings govern analysis for member accounts and members cannot review or change them, and only the administrator has direct access to the sensitive data findings automated discovery produces while members retain read access to statistics for their own buckets.
svg.title: A sensitivity score is a statement about what was sampled
svg.text: A score of 50 is two different facts wearing the same label.
Macie automated sensitive data discovery — a daily sample, and a number built from what it reached.
The daily cycle — it samples, and AWS says so plainly
Groups objects with similar metadata that are “likely to have similar content” — by bucket name, prefix,
storage class, file name extension, last modified date — then takes a representative set from each group.
“Any single object sample isn’t guaranteed to be conclusive.”
Breadth-first on purpose: a bucket not yet analysed outranks one already known to hold sensitive data.
An object analysed once and unchanged since is never analysed again. Results begin to appear within 48 hours.
One value, two unrelated situations
50 · Not yet analyzed
Assigned to every bucket on enablement.
A queue position. Resolves on its own,
in a day or two.
50 · Not yet analyzed
“If an S3 bucket’s permissions settings
prevent Macie from accessing” it.
Never resolves. Same row.
What moves the number
finds sensitive data in an object → increases
finds none in an object → decreases
object later changed or deleted → detections
removed from the score
So a falling score and a cleanup look identical.
What the score is, by definition
“the intersection of two primary dimensions:”
· how much sensitive data Macie found
· how much data Macie analysed
Two dimensions, one number — so “looked hard, found
little” and “barely looked” are not distinguishable.
Four populations the inventory does not speak for
Not classifiable — unsupported storage class, or no file name extension for a supported format
Encrypted beyond reach — analysable “only if” the key is one Macie can access and is allowed to use
Excluded by you — up to 1,000 buckets
A whole Region — settings “apply only to the current AWS Region”, so it produces no rows at all
The one confident absence
An empty bucket scores 1, label Not sensitive.
Macie does separate “nothing here” from “not looked” — when it can.
The override tells you what it is for
Assign 100 by hand and the label is Sensitive.
An input to judgement, not a substitute for it.
Score and label “don’t imply or otherwise indicate the criticality or importance” of the bucket — AWS’s words, worth quoting.
Age every 50. Past a couple of days it is a bucket policy or a key policy, not a result.
In an organisation only the administrator sees the findings — so remediation is a relay, not a dashboard.
